title: Found doing this
hook: let death find me attending to my will, Epictetus says (Discourses 3.5)

segments.voice: Yesterday: three fields, desire, action and assent, and your line, let each door open for a few breaths. Which field did you choose to train? Day four hundred eighteen.

I'm sick here, one of Epictetus' students says, and I want to go home. Not an unreasonable wish: if I'm going to be sick, or worse, let it be in my own bed. Epictetus answers with questions. And they lead him into a quiet passage of the Discourses, about what any of us would want to be doing when the end comes. It's less grim than it sounds. Today: found doing this.
screen: `A SICK STUDENT WANTS TO GO HOME.` → `LET IT BE IN MY OWN BED.` → `LESS GRIM THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter five, to students who leave because of illness. Epictetus asks the student a few practical questions. Would you be in less danger at home? Is there no fever there? And then he widens the question. Where, and doing what, would you like death to find you? It's going to find each of us somewhere, doing something. A farmer at his farming. A trader at his trade. An official in office. Epictetus says what he would choose. Let it find me, he says, attending to nothing but my own will: keeping it calm, unhindered, unforced, free. He wants to be found practicing. And he imagines being able to say, at the end, that he used well what he'd been given: that he didn't misuse his mind, never complained of his lot, kept his commitments. That's the heart of the passage, and it isn't really about death. It's about now. If you'd want to be found doing something, you can be doing it already, today, in ordinary places. Not something grand. Being patient with the person in front of you. Doing your work honestly. Treating your own mind with care. Epictetus' answer is simple enough to carry into a kitchen or an office: whatever I'm doing, let it be something I'd be glad to be found doing.
screen: `WOULD YOU BE SAFER AT HOME?` · `IT WILL FIND YOU SOMEWHERE.` · `FOUND ATTENDING TO MY WILL.` · `IT'S REALLY ABOUT NOW.` · then, large: `FOUND DOING THIS.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. This doesn't need to be heavy. Ask yourself, simply: what would I be glad to be found doing? Let an answer come: being kind, finishing a piece of honest work, laughing with someone, sitting quietly like this. Then look at the next few hours of your day. Where could you do that thing, even in a small way? Choose one place. The bell holds the time.
Found doing this. Epictetus' answer to where he'd want death to find him: attending to his own will, keeping it calm and free, which means living that way now.
Your line: found doing this. Today, do one thing you'd be glad to be found doing, and do it on purpose. Day four hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners ask each morning what they would want to be found doing, and use the answer to choose how to spend part of the day.

fork.setup: a student, ill and far from home, wants to leave school. you're Epictetus. what do you ask?
options: where, and doing what, would you like death to find you?
fork.reveal: after a few practical questions, he turns to the larger one, and answers it himself: attending to my will, keeping it free.

trapdoor: what you thought: think about death so you'll be afraid of wasting time.
what it means: decide what you'd want to be found doing, and do it now, in ordinary places.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus returns to this theme in 4.10, and the 'meditation on death' (meletē thanatou) goes back to Plato's Phaedo.

notes: Discourses 3.5 paraphrased: the sick student who wants to go home; 'was there no fever at home?'; what we want to be doing when death finds us (farmer, merchant); 'may death find me attending to my will, untroubled, unhindered, unconstrained, free'; the address to God about the faculties received (described, not quoted, since it is prayer-like). Confirm details, especially the farmer/merchant list (which may be from 4.10).
Plato, Phaedo 67e/81a ('practice for dying') named in the trapdoor; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook drops the unsourced 'at Nicopolis', 'far from his family', 'Epictetus understood that' and the superlative 'one of the most quietly powerful passages'; cut 'as he always does' and the sweeping 'people in many traditions'; death's list now follows 3.5 (farming, trading, holding office) rather than an added gardener; 'didn't blame anyone' became 'never complained of his lot', since in 3.5 the complaint he disowns is against God.
